title: Thank You for Your Candor
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article explores why candor is chronically underused in teams despite its clear value, tracing the reluctance to a basic desire to be liked and to avoid the vulnerability of exposing what one doesn't know. While acknowledging that popular ideas like radical candor can tip into offensive bluntness, the author argues most teams actually suffer from too little candor, not too much. The piece recommends specific leader behaviors to draw more candor out of others: thanking people for candid input, sometimes even in advance of a discussion, and explicitly granting permission to be frank. These small acts, the author argues, shift the social calculus so that being honest feels safer than staying silent.
points: Most people withhold candid views to avoid seeming unlikeable or exposing gaps in their knowledge.
Despite popular warnings about radical candor going too far, most teams actually suffer from too little of it.
Leaders who are themselves direct and reward candor in others tend to receive more of it.
Thanking people for candid input, sometimes proactively, reliably encourages more of it.
Explicitly granting permission to be frank makes it easier for others to risk being disliked.
quotes: Being forthright with your views and frank in the way you express them can hurt others’ feelings and make you unlikeable.
Candor is the secret ingredient when it comes to addressing important issues.
The unfortunate reality is we really don’t like people who are too transparent or uncensored.
We need more candor, especially when performance matters. Which is just about always.
Thanking people for their candidness before responding is a habit of great leaders.
People need to know that the leader prizes candor and wants it.
